title: More Than Revenue: What Actually Decides the Right Level of Fractional CFO Support
linkedin:
Two businesses turn over the same revenue this year. One needs a fractional CFO in the room once a month. The other needs them every week.

That is not a hypothetical. It is the pattern we see constantly among owner-led businesses along the East Coast.

Revenue is the number most owners reach for when sizing this kind of support, because it is easy to compare and easy to bracket. But revenue says nothing about how many live decisions are actually on the table in a given quarter.

A steady $12 million business with a settled customer base and predictable margins can run comfortably on a monthly rhythm. A $4 million business that is hiring every quarter, testing a price change, opening a second site and weighing up funding all at once needs someone at the table far more often, regardless of what the top line says.

Getting the level wrong runs quietly in both directions. Too light, and the biggest decisions get made solo in the gaps between contact. Too heavy, and the business pays for a cadence of conversation the pace of change does not actually require.

The honest sizing question is not how big is the business. It is how many decisions is it about to make.

Quick one for the business owners here: if you brought in extra financial support tomorrow, would you use it every week, or would monthly check-ins be plenty?

We ask because the businesses that get the most out of a fractional CFO are not always the biggest ones. They are the ones with the most decisions actually in motion right now: hiring, pricing, a new site, a funding conversation.

Two businesses can turn over exactly the same revenue and need completely different levels of support. Worth thinking about before you size it by the top line alone.

A question we hear often from business owners across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria: how much financial support does my business actually need?

The instinct is usually to size it by revenue. A bigger business assumes it needs more involvement, a smaller one assumes it can get by with less. In our experience, that is not the number that matters most.

What actually decides the right level of support is how many real decisions are on the table in a given quarter. A steady business with a settled customer base and predictable margins can run well on a light, monthly rhythm. A business that is hiring, testing a price change, opening a new location or weighing up funding all in the same few months usually needs a more frequent level of involvement, no matter what its revenue looks like.

Getting this wrong tends to happen quietly in both directions: either too little support while the big decisions get made solo, or paying for a level of involvement the business is not yet moving fast enough to use.

If your business has a few of these decisions coming up over the next quarter, it is worth working out which end of that range you actually sit on. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
